lead: This unit is the dynamics half of mechanics: why particles move the way they do. You first learn to describe motion without asking its cause (kinematics), then connect force, energy and momentum to that motion (kinetics). After it you can find the velocity, acceleration, time, distance, force or post-collision speed in any particle problem these syllabi set.
about: The unit starts with the simplest case, a particle on a straight line (5.1), and builds the derivative and integral links between position, velocity and acceleration. Chapter 5.2 bends the path: velocity stays tangent to it, acceleration splits into tangential and normal parts, and polar coordinates give radial and transverse parts. Projectile motion (5.3) is the standard curved-path problem with constant acceleration. Chapter 5.4 covers motion measured from a moving frame, and motion limited by strings and contacts. The kinetics chapters then add the cause: Newton's second law with D'Alembert's trick (5.5), the work-energy route (5.6), the impulse-momentum route (5.7), and impact (5.8), where two bodies exchange momentum in a very short time.

chapters.idea: On a straight line, position, velocity and acceleration are linked by differentiation and integration, and constant acceleration is the one case with ready-made formulas.
chapters.depth: Position s, velocity v = ds/dt, acceleration a = dv/dt = v dv/ds; fix a positive direction once and keep it. Uniform acceleration: derive and use v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as, and mean velocity (u + v)/2. Variable acceleration in three forms: a = f(t), a = f(v), a = f(s). Solve each by separating variables and applying the initial conditions; for a = f(v) use dv/f(v) = dt, for a = f(s) use v dv = a ds. Read s-t, v-t and a-t graphs: slope of s-t is v, area under v-t is the distance travelled. Some syllabi call this 'motion in a straight line' or 'rectilinear translation'.

figure.aria: Velocity rises steadily from zero to 10 m/s at t = 20 s, then falls steadily to zero at t = 30 s; the area under the two straight segments is the total distance of 150 m.

chapters.example: A train starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 0.5 m/s² for 20 s. It then brakes uniformly at 1 m/s² until it stops. Find the maximum velocity, the total time and the total distance covered. Answer: v_max = 0.5 × 20 = 10 m/s; braking time = 10/1 = 10 s, so total time = 30 s; distance in the first stage = ½ × 0.5 × 20² = 100 m, in the second = ½ × 10 × 10 = 50 m, total 150 m.
chapters.trap: Using v = u + at when a is not constant, and dropping signs: during braking a is negative but v keeps its sign, so s keeps increasing.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for units and vector sense; school calculus for differentiation and integration.
chapters.leave: Curved paths to 5.2; the cause of the acceleration to 5.5.

chapters.idea: Velocity is always along the tangent to the path, and acceleration splits into a part that changes speed and a part that changes direction.
chapters.depth: Velocity magnitude v = ds/dt, directed along the tangent. Normal-tangential (path) components: a_t = dv/dt along the tangent, a_n = v²/ρ along the inward normal, where ρ is the radius of curvature at that point; total a = √(a_t² + a_n²), at an angle tan⁻¹(a_n/a_t) from the tangent. Rectangular components a_x = ẍ, a_y = ÿ for plane motion. Radial-transverse (polar) components: a_r = r̈ − rθ̇² and a_θ = rθ̈ + 2ṙθ̇; read each term — r̈ is the radial speeding up, −rθ̇² is the inward turning term and 2ṙθ̇ comes from both radius and angle changing. Some syllabi call these intrinsic coordinates or path variables.

figure.title: Acceleration on a curved path
figure.aria: The velocity of a particle splits into a tangential part that changes its speed and a normal part that changes its direction, and the two add as perpendicular vectors to give the total acceleration.

chapters.example: A car enters a curve of radius 50 m at 20 m/s and the driver is still pressing the accelerator, so the speed is rising at 3 m/s². Find the magnitude and direction of the total acceleration at that instant. Answer: a_n = 20²/50 = 8 m/s² towards the centre of the curve, a_t = 3 m/s² along the tangent; a = √(9 + 64) = √73 = 8.54 m/s², at tan⁻¹(8/3) = 69.4° from the tangent, leaning towards the centre of curvature.
chapters.trap: Using a_n = v²/r only for circles; on any curved path use the radius of curvature at that point. Also a_n points to the centre of curvature, never away from it.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for v = ds/dt; Unit 1 for resolving vectors at right angles.
chapters.leave: Rotation of a rigid body about a fixed axis to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A projectile is two independent straight-line motions at once: constant velocity horizontally, constant acceleration g vertically.
chapters.depth: Launch speed u at angle θ to the horizontal, no air resistance. Horizontal: x = u cosθ · t. Vertical: y = u sinθ · t − ½gt², v_y = u sinθ − gt. Eliminate t to get the equation of the trajectory, y = x tanθ − gx²/(2u² cos²θ), which is a parabola. For level ground: time of flight 2u sinθ/g, horizontal range u² sin2θ/g, maximum height u² sin²θ/(2g); the range is largest at θ = 45°. Horizontal projection from a height as a special case: time from √(2h/g), range u√(2h/g). Only a few universities teach this as a separate topic, so keep it short.

figure.aria: Parabolic path of a ball launched at 20 m/s and 30 degrees, peaking at 5.10 m halfway along and landing 35.3 m away.

chapters.example: A ball is kicked from level ground at 20 m/s at 30° to the horizontal. Find the time of flight, the maximum height and the horizontal range (take g = 9.81 m/s²). Answer: flight time = 2 × 20 × sin30°/9.81 = 2.04 s; height = (20 sin30°)²/(2 × 9.81) = 100/19.62 = 5.10 m; range = 20² × sin60°/9.81 = 400 × 0.866/9.81 = 35.3 m.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that u cosθ stays constant, and using the range formula when the landing point is not at the same height as the launch point.
chapters.prereq: 5.1 for the vertical motion and 5.2 for the components.
chapters.leave: Air resistance and spinning balls are out of scope; general curved paths to 5.2.

chapters.idea: Velocities and accelerations are always measured from some frame, and a string or a contact between bodies ties their motions together.
chapters.depth: Translating frames: v_A = v_B + v_A/B and a_A = a_B + a_A/B, where v_A/B is the velocity of A as seen from B; the frame must translate, not rotate. Standard problems: rain seen through a moving window, a swimmer crossing a river with a current, two vehicles on perpendicular roads, a boat heading upstream. Constrained motion: a string, a cable or a contact removes freedom, so the system has one degree of freedom. Write the total length of the string in terms of coordinates measured from a fixed datum, differentiate once for velocities and twice for accelerations. Cover block-and-pulley systems, two blocks joined over a pulley on inclines, and a ladder against a wall.

figure.title: Rain seen from a moving car
figure.aria: Vertical rain velocity and horizontal car velocity combine by vector subtraction into a relative velocity of 18.0 m/s tilted 56.3 degrees from the vertical.

chapters.example: Rain falls vertically at 10 m/s. A car moves horizontally at 15 m/s. Find the magnitude and direction of the velocity of the rain as seen by the driver. Answer: v_rel = v_rain − v_car = (−15, −10) m/s, magnitude √(15² + 10²) = √325 = 18.0 m/s, angled at tan⁻¹(15/10) = 56.3° from the vertical, appearing to come at the windscreen from the front.
chapters.trap: Subtracting in the wrong order (v_A/B is the velocity of A measured by B, so its sign is opposite to v_B/A), and measuring the string length from a moving pulley instead of a fixed datum.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for vector subtraction; 5.1 for differentiating position with respect to time.
chapters.leave: Rotating frames and Coriolis acceleration are outside this syllabus; relative motion of points on a rigid body to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: In an inertial frame the net force on a particle equals mass times its acceleration, and adding the inertia force −ma turns the same equation into a statics problem.
chapters.depth: Newton's second law ΣF = ma, valid only in an inertial (non-accelerating) frame. Draw the free body diagram first, then write components: rectangular (ΣF_x = ma_x, ΣF_y = ma_y), normal-tangential (ΣF_t = ma_t, ΣF_n = ma_n) and cylindrical (ΣF_r = ma_r, ΣF_θ = ma_θ, ΣF_z = ma_z). Rough surfaces bring in friction from Unit 3. D'Alembert's principle: add a fictitious inertia force of magnitude ma opposite to the acceleration, and the body is in 'dynamic equilibrium', Σ(F − ma) = 0, so all the tools of statics apply. For a system of particles ΣF_ext = m_total a_cm: the centre of mass moves like one particle carrying the whole mass.

figure.title: Crate pulled at 30°
figure.aria: The chain from the crate to the answer: draw the free body diagram, use vertical equilibrium to get the normal force, apply Newton's second law horizontally, and read off the acceleration.

chapters.example: A 50 kg crate on a horizontal floor is pulled by a rope at 30° above the horizontal with tension 200 N. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.25. Find the acceleration (g = 9.81 m/s²). Answer: vertical equilibrium gives N = mg − T sin30° = 490.5 − 100 = 390.5 N; friction = 0.25 × 390.5 = 97.6 N; horizontal force = 200 cos30° = 173.2 N; net = 173.2 − 97.6 = 75.6 N; a = 75.6/50 = 1.51 m/s².
chapters.trap: Drawing the inertia force and the real forces on one diagram and then also writing ΣF = ma, which counts ma twice. Also the normal reaction drops when the pull has an upward component, so friction drops too.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for free body diagrams and resolution; Unit 3 for friction; 5.1 to 5.4 for the acceleration terms.
chapters.leave: Euler's equations and the kinetics of rigid bodies to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: The work done by all forces on a particle equals the change in its kinetic energy, and for conservative forces this becomes a stored potential energy that can be traded back and forth.
chapters.depth: Work of a constant force U = F d cosα; of a variable force U = ∫F·dr along the path; of weight −W Δy; of a spring −½k(x₂² − x₁²). Work of kinetic friction is negative and depends on the path length. Power P = dU/dt = F·v. Kinetic energy T = ½mv². Work-energy principle U₁₋₂ = T₂ − T₁, first for one particle, then for a system of particles. Conservative forces depend only on position: they have a potential energy V with F = −dV/ds, and T₁ + V₁ = T₂ + V₂ (conservation of mechanical energy). Alternative form for non-conservative forces: U₁₋₂ = ΔT + ΔV. Some syllabi call V the potential function or the conservative force field.

figure.title: Energy bookkeeping
figure.aria: A block slides from rest down a smooth incline reaching 7.0 m/s at the bottom, then friction on a rough patch brings it to rest after 8.33 m.

chapters.example: A 2 kg block starts from rest and slides 5 m down a smooth incline of 30° to the horizontal. It then meets a rough horizontal floor with μ = 0.3. Find its speed at the bottom of the incline and the distance it slides before stopping (g = 9.81 m/s²). Answer: height fallen = 5 sin30° = 2.5 m; ½v² = gh gives v = √(2 × 9.81 × 2.5) = 7.0 m/s; on the floor ½v² = μgd, so d = 49.05/(2 × 0.3 × 9.81) = 8.33 m.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to fix a datum for potential energy, and giving friction positive work. Energy gives speed only, never direction.
chapters.prereq: 5.5 for forces and free body diagrams; Unit 3 for friction; 5.1 for the kinematic equations.
chapters.leave: Strain energy and vibrations to Unit 6; virtual work to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Force integrated over time gives impulse, which equals the change in momentum, and with no external impulse the momentum does not change.
chapters.depth: Linear impulse I = ∫F dt, a vector in N·s, equal to the area under the force-time graph; average force = I/Δt. Impulse-momentum principle: mv₁ + ∫F dt = mv₂, component by component. Momentum is conserved in a direction when the external impulse in that direction is zero. For a system of particles ΣF_ext = d(Σmv)/dt, so recoil, explosion and bullet-into-block problems follow. Moment of momentum (angular momentum) about a point O: H_O = r × mv; the moment-of-momentum equation ΣM_O = dH_O/dt, and for a central force H_O is constant (conservation of angular momentum).

figure.aria: A triangular force-time pulse peaking at 2100 N; the area under it is the impulse of 10.5 N·s delivered to the ball.

chapters.example: A cricket ball of mass 0.15 kg arrives at 30 m/s and is hit straight back along the same line at 40 m/s. The bat is in contact for 0.01 s. Find the impulse and the average force. Answer: take the outgoing direction as positive, so v₁ = −30 m/s and v₂ = +40 m/s; impulse = m(v₂ − v₁) = 0.15 × 70 = 10.5 N·s; average force = 10.5/0.01 = 1050 N.
chapters.trap: Signs: a ball hit straight back has a change of velocity equal to the sum of the speeds, not the difference. Also impulse is the whole area under the force-time graph, not the peak force times time.
chapters.prereq: 5.5 for F = ma; 5.2 for resolving a vector into components.
chapters.leave: Angular impulse and angular momentum of rigid bodies to Unit 6; coefficient of restitution to 5.8.

chapters.idea: In a collision momentum is conserved along the line of impact, and the coefficient of restitution fixes how much of the relative speed along that line is returned.
chapters.depth: Two bodies collide over a very short time, so the internal impulse dominates and total momentum is conserved. Line of impact: the common normal at the point of contact. Central impact means both centres of mass lie on the line of impact. Direct (head-on) central impact: all velocities are along that line. Coefficient of restitution e = (v₂′ − v₁′)/(v₁ − v₂), with 0 ≤ e ≤ 1; e = 1 is perfectly elastic, e = 0 perfectly plastic (they move together after). Solve every problem with two equations: momentum and restitution. Oblique central impact: resolve each velocity along and perpendicular to the line of impact; the perpendicular components are unchanged, momentum is conserved along the line, and restitution applies along the line only. Energy lost = T_before − T_after.

figure.title: Direct central impact, e = 0.5

nodes.label: Before
nodes.note: 4 kg at 6 m/s, 2 kg at 3 m/s

figure.aria: Two equations settle a collision: momentum conservation supplies the sum of the final momenta and restitution supplies the difference of the final velocities, giving both answers.

chapters.example: Ball A of mass 4 kg moving at 6 m/s overtakes ball B of mass 2 kg moving at 3 m/s along the same line. The coefficient of restitution is 0.5. Find the velocities just after impact. Answer: momentum 4(6) + 2(3) = 30 kg·m/s, so 4v₁′ + 2v₂′ = 30; restitution v₂′ − v₁′ = 0.5(6 − 3) = 1.5 m/s. Solving gives v₁′ = 4.5 m/s and v₂′ = 6.0 m/s. Kinetic energy falls from 81 J to 76.5 J, which is correct because e is below 1.
chapters.trap: Applying restitution to the components perpendicular to the line of impact — those simply pass through unchanged. Also fix one positive direction along the line and use it for all four velocities.
chapters.prereq: 5.7 for impulse-momentum; 5.2 for resolving along and normal to a line.
chapters.leave: Impact of rigid bodies with rotation and angular impulse to Unit 6.

links: straight-line v and a become the tangential components on a curve
projectile motion is curvilinear motion under constant acceleration g
relative velocity is built by subtracting velocity vectors
Newton's second law turns the acceleration of 5.1 into a force
integrating force over displacement gives the work-energy principle
integrating force over time gives the impulse-momentum principle
two routes from the same second law: energy is scalar, momentum is vector
impact is impulse-momentum plus a coefficient of restitution
